{{Short description|Mathematical representation}}
In [[mathematics]] the '''Burau representation''' is a [[group representation|representation]] of the [[braid group]]s, named after and originally studied by the German mathematician Werner Burau<ref name="burau">{{cite journal| last=Burau| first=Werner| year=1936 |title=Über Zopfgruppen und gleichsinnig verdrillte Verkettungen|journal=Abh. Math. Sem. Univ. Hamburg|volume=11|pages=179–186| doi=10.1007/bf02940722| s2cid=119576586}}</ref> during the 1930s.  The '''Burau representation''' has two common and near-equivalent formulations, the '''reduced''' and '''unreduced''' Burau representations.

== Definition ==
[[File:InfiniteCyclicCovering.gif|thumb|300px|The covering space {{math|''C<sub>n</sub>''}} may be thought of concretely as follows: cut the disk along lines from the boundary to the marked points. Take as many copies of the result as there are integers, stack them vertically, and connect them by ramps going from one side of the cut on one level to the other side of the cut on the level below. This procedure is shown here for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}}; the covering transformations {{math|''t''<sup>±1</sup>}} act by shifting the space vertically.]]
Consider the [[braid group]] {{math|''B<sub>n</sub>''}} to be the [[mapping class group]] of a disc with {{mvar|n}} marked points {{math|'''D'''<sub>''n''</sub>}}. The [[homology group]] {{math|''H''<sub>1</sub>('''D'''<sub>''n''</sub>)}} is free abelian of rank {{mvar|n}}.  Moreover, the invariant subspace of {{math|''H''<sub>1</sub>('''D'''<sub>''n''</sub>)}} (under the action of {{math|''B<sub>n</sub>''}}) is primitive and infinite cyclic.  Let {{math|''π'' : ''H''<sub>1</sub>('''D'''<sub>''n''</sub>) → '''Z'''}} be the projection onto this invariant subspace.  Then there is a [[covering space]] {{math|''C<sub>n</sub>''}} corresponding to this projection map.  Much as in the construction of the [[Alexander polynomial]], consider {{math|''H''<sub>1</sub>(''C<sub>n</sub>'')}} as a module over the group-ring of covering transformations {{math|'''Z'''['''Z''']}}, which is isomorphic to the ring of  [[Laurent polynomial]]s {{math|'''Z'''[''t'', ''t''<sup>−1</sup>]}}. As a {{math|'''Z'''[''t'', ''t''<sup>−1</sup>]}}-module, {{math|''H''<sub>1</sub>(''C<sub>n</sub>'')}} is free of rank {{math|''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1}}.  By the basic theory of [[covering space]]s, {{math|''B<sub>n</sub>''}} acts on {{math|''H''<sub>1</sub>(''C<sub>n</sub>'')}}, and this representation is called the ''reduced Burau representation''.

The ''unreduced Burau representation'' has a similar definition, namely one replaces {{math|'''D'''<sub>''n''</sub>}} with its [[blowing up|(real, oriented) blow-up]] at the marked points.  Then instead of considering {{math|''H''<sub>1</sub>(''C<sub>n</sub>'')}} one considers the relative homology {{math|''H''<sub>1</sub>(''C<sub>n</sub>'', Γ)}} where {{math|''γ'' ⊂ '''D'''<sub>''n''</sub>}} is the part of the boundary of {{math|'''D'''<sub>''n''</sub>}} corresponding to the blow-up operation together with one point on the disc's boundary. {{math|Γ}} denotes the lift of {{math|''γ''}} to {{math|''C<sub>n</sub>''}}.  As a {{math|'''Z'''[''t'', ''t''<sup>−1</sup>]}}-module this is free of rank {{mvar|n}}.

By the [[homology (mathematics)|homology long exact sequence of a pair]], the Burau representations fit into a short exact sequence

:{{math|0 → ''V<sub>r</sub>'' → ''V<sub>u</sub>'' → ''D'' ⊕ '''Z'''[''t'', ''t''<sup>−1</sup>] → 0,}}

where {{math|''V<sub>r</sub>''}} (resp. {{math|''V<sub>u</sub>''}}) is the reduced (resp. unreduced) Burau {{math|''B<sub>n</sub>''}}-module and {{math|''D'' ⊂ '''Z'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} is the complement to the diagonal subspace, in other words:

:<math>D = \left \{ \left (x_1,\cdots,x_n \right ) \in \mathbf{Z}^n : x_1+\cdots+x_n=0 \right \},</math>

and {{math|''B<sub>n</sub>''}} acts on {{math|'''Z'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} by the permutation representation.

== Explicit matrices ==
Let {{math|''&sigma;''<sub>''i''</sub>}} denote the standard generators of the braid group {{math|''B''<sub>''n''</sub>}}. Then the unreduced Burau representation may be given explicitly by mapping

<math display=block>\sigma_i \mapsto \left( \begin{array}{c|cc|c} I_{i-1} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \hline 0 & 1-t & t & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 & I_{n-i-1} \end{array} \right),</math>

for {{math|1 ≤ ''i'' ≤ ''n'' &minus; 1}}, where {{math|''I''<sub>''k''</sub>}} denotes the {{math|''k'' &times; ''k''}} identity matrix. Likewise, for {{math|''n'' ≥ 3}} the reduced Burau representation is given by

<math display=block>\begin{align}
\sigma_1 &\mapsto \left( \begin{array}{cc|c}-t & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \hline 0 & 0 & I_{n-3} \end{array} \right), \\[3pt]
\sigma_i &\mapsto \left( \begin{array}{c|ccc|c} I_{i-2} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \hline 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & t & -t & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & I_{n-i-2} \end{array} \right), \quad 2 \leq i \leq n-2, \\[3pt]
\sigma_{n-1} &\mapsto \left( \begin{array}{c|cc} I_{n-3} & 0 & 0 \\ \hline 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & t & -t \end{array} \right),
\end{align}</math>
while for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 2}}, it maps
<math display=block>\sigma_1 \mapsto \left( -t \right).</math>

=== Bowling alley interpretation ===
[[Vaughan Jones]]<ref name="Jones">{{cite journal| last=Jones| first=Vaughan| year=1987 |title=Hecke algebra representations of Braid Groups and Link Polynomials|journal=Annals of Mathematics |series=Second Series|volume=126| issue =  2|pages=335–388| doi=10.2307/1971403| jstor=1971403}}</ref> gave the following interpretation of the unreduced Burau representation of positive braids for {{math|''t''}} in {{math|[0,1]}}  &ndash; i.e. for braids that are words in the standard braid group generators containing no inverses &ndash; which follows immediately from the above explicit description:

Given a positive braid {{math|''&sigma;''}} on {{math|''n''}} strands, interpret it as a bowling alley with {{math|''n''}} intertwining lanes. Now throw a bowling ball down one of the lanes and assume that at every crossing where its path crosses over another lane, it falls down with probability {{math|''t''}} and continues along the lower lane. Then the {{math|(''i'',''j'')}}'th entry of the unreduced Burau representation of {{math|''&sigma;''}} is the probability that a ball thrown into the {{math|''i''}}'th lane ends up in the {{math|''j''}}'th lane.

== Relation to the Alexander polynomial ==
If a knot {{mvar|K}} is the closure of a braid {{mvar|f}} in {{math|''B''<sub>''n''</sub>}}, then, up to multiplication by a unit in {{math|'''Z'''[''t'', ''t''<sup>−1</sup>]}}, the [[Alexander polynomial]] {{math|&Delta;<sub>''K''</sub>(''t'')}} of {{math|''K''}} is given by
:<math>\frac{1-t}{1-t^n} \det(I-f_*),</math>
where {{math|''f''<sub>∗</sub>}} is the reduced Burau representation of the braid {{mvar|f}}.

For example, if {{math|''f'' {{=}} ''&sigma;''<sub>1</sub>''&sigma;''<sub>2</sub>}} in {{math|''B''<sub>3</sub>}}, one finds by using the explicit matrices above that
: <math>\frac{1-t}{1-t^n} \det(I-f_*) = 1,</math>
and the closure of {{math|''f''<sub>*</sub>}} is the unknot whose Alexander polynomial is {{math|1}}.

== Faithfulness ==
The first nonfaithful Burau representations were found by John A. Moody without the use of computer, using a notion of [[winding number]] or contour integration.<ref>{{citation| last=Moody | first=John Atwell| author-link=John Atwell Moody|title= The faithfulness question for the Burau representation| journal= [[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume= 119 |year=1993|issue= 2|pages= 671–679|doi=10.1090/s0002-9939-1993-1158006-x|mr=1158006| jstor=2159956|doi-access=free}}</ref> A more conceptual understanding, due to Darren D. Long and Mark Paton<ref name="lp">{{citation| last1=Long |first1=Darren D.| last2=Paton|first2=Mark| title= The Burau representation is not faithful for <math>n \ge 6</math> | journal=[[Topology (journal)|Topology]] |volume= 32 | year=1993|issue=2|pages=439–447|doi=10.1016/0040-9383(93)90030-Y|mr=1217079|doi-access=free}}</ref> interprets the linking or winding as coming from [[Poincaré duality]] in first homology relative to the basepoint of a covering space, and uses the [[Poincaré duality|intersection form]] (traditionally called Squier's Form as Craig Squier was the first to explore its properties).<ref name="squier">{{cite journal|last=Squier|first=Craig C|year=1984|title=The Burau representation is unitary|journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]| volume=90 |issue=2 |pages=199–202 | doi=10.2307/2045338|jstor=2045338|doi-access=free}}</ref>  [[Stephen Bigelow]] combined computer techniques and the Long–Paton theorem to show that the Burau representation is not faithful for {{math|''n'' ≥ 5}}.<ref name="bigelow">{{cite journal| last=Bigelow |first=Stephen|author-link= Stephen Bigelow |year=1999 |title=The Burau representation is not faithful for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}}|journal=[[Geometry & Topology]] |volume=3|pages=397–404| doi=10.2140/gt.1999.3.397|arxiv=math/9904100|s2cid=5967061}}</ref><ref name="icm">[[S. Bigelow]], [https://www.ams.org/notices/200301/comm-icm2002.pdf International Congress of Mathematicians, Beijing, 2002]</ref><ref>[[Vladimir Turaev]], [http://archive.numdam.org/article/SB_1999-2000__42__389_0.pdf Faithful representations of the braid groups, Bourbaki 1999-2000]</ref> Bigelow moreover provides an explicit non-trivial element in the kernel as a word in the standard generators of the braid group: let
:<math>\psi_1 = \sigma_3^{-1}\sigma_2 \sigma_1^2 \sigma_2 \sigma_4^3 \sigma_3 \sigma_2, \quad \psi_2 = \sigma_4^{-1} \sigma_3 \sigma_2 \sigma_1^{-2} \sigma_2 \sigma_1^2 \sigma_2^2 \sigma_1 \sigma_4^5.</math>
Then an element of the kernel is given by the commutator
:<math>[\psi_1^{-1}\sigma_4\psi_1,\psi_2^{-1}\sigma_4\sigma_3\sigma_2\sigma_1^2\sigma_2\sigma_3\sigma_4\psi_2].</math>

The Burau representation for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 2}} has been known to be faithful for some time, as the braid group is infinite cyclic.  The {{math|''n'' {{=}} 3}} case was shown to be faithful by Magnus–Peluso in 1969.<ref>{{citation| last = Birman | first = Joan S. | author-link = Joan Birman| isbn = 978-0-691-08149-6| mr = 0375281| location = Princeton, N.J.| publisher = [[Princeton University Press]]| series = Annals of Mathematics Studies| title = Braids, links, and mapping class groups|title-link= Braids, Links, and Mapping Class Groups | volume = 82| year = 1974 | page = 129}}</ref> The faithfulness of the Burau representation when {{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}} has long been an [[open problem]].  In 2026 Vasudha Bharathram, [[Joan Birman]], and [[Tara E. Brendle]] posted a preprinton [[arXiv]] claiming to prove faithfulness for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}}.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Bharathram |first1=Vasudha |title=The Burau representation of the braid group is faithful for n = 4 |date=2026-07-06 |eprint=2607.05283 |last2=Birman |first2=Joan S. |last3=Brendle |first3=Tara E. |class=math.GT }}</ref> However, as noted by the ''New York Times'', it will take time for mathematicians to certify the proposed solution.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Barber |first=Gregory |date=2026-09-06 |title=The 92-Year-Old Mathematician and the Teenage Apprentice |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/06/science/92-year-old-mathematician-apprentice.html |access-date=2026-09-06 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

The Burau representation appears as a summand of the [[Jones representation]], and for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}}, the faithfulness of the Burau representation is equivalent to that of the Jones representation, which on the other hand is related to the question of whether or not the [[Jones polynomial]] is an [[Unknotting problem|unknot detector]].<ref name="bigelowunknot">{{cite journal| last=Bigelow |first=Stephen|author-link= Stephen Bigelow |year=2002 |title=Does the Jones polynomial detect the unknot?|journal=[[Journal of Knot Theory and Its Ramifications]] |volume=11|number=4|pages=493–505 |doi=10.1142/s0218216502001779|arxiv=math/0012086|s2cid=1353805}}</ref>

== Geometry ==
Craig Squier showed that the Burau representation preserves a [[sesquilinear form]].<ref name="squier"/>  Moreover, when the variable {{mvar|t}} is chosen to be a transcendental [[unit complex number]] near {{math|1}}, it is a positive-definite [[Sesquilinear form#Hermitian form|Hermitian pairing]]. Thus the Burau representation of the braid group {{math|''B<sub>n</sub>''}} can be thought of as a map into the [[unitary group]] U(''n'').
